{{short description|Topological game}}
The '''Choquet game''' is a [[topological game]] named after [[Gustave Choquet]], who was in 1969 the first to investigate such games.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Choquet|first1=Gustave|title=Lectures on Analysis: Integration and topological vector spaces|date=1969|publisher=W. A. Benjamin|isbn=9780805369601|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tVz_RQAACAAJ|language=en}}</ref> A closely related game is known as the '''strong Choquet game'''.

Let <math>X</math> be a non-empty [[topological space]]. The Choquet game of <math>X</math>, <math>G(X)</math>, is defined as follows: Player I chooses <math>U_0</math>, a non-empty [[Open set|open subset]] of <math>X</math>, then Player II chooses <math>V_0</math>, a non-empty open subset of <math>U_0</math>, then Player I chooses <math>U_1</math>, a non-empty open subset of <math>V_0</math>, etc. The players continue this process, constructing a sequence <math>U_0 \supseteq V_0 \supseteq U_1 \supseteq V_1 \supseteq U_2 ...</math>.

If <math>\bigcap\limits_{i=0}^{\infty} U_i = \emptyset</math> then Player I wins, otherwise Player II wins.

It was proven by [[John C. Oxtoby]] that a non-empty topological space <math>X</math> is a [[Baire space]] if and only if Player I has no [[winning strategy]]. A nonempty topological space <math>X</math> in which Player II has a winning strategy is called a '''Choquet space'''. (Note that it is possible that neither player has a winning strategy.) Thus every Choquet space is Baire. On the other hand, there are Baire spaces (even [[Separable space|separable]] [[metrizable]] ones) that are not Choquet spaces, so the converse fails.

The strong Choquet game of <math>X</math>, <math>G^s(X)</math>, is defined similarly, except that Player I chooses <math>(x_0,U_0)</math>, then Player II chooses <math>V_0</math>, then Player I chooses <math>(x_1,U_1)</math>, etc, such that <math>x_i \in U_i, V_i</math> for all <math>i</math>. A topological space <math>X</math> in which Player II has a winning strategy for <math>G^s(X)</math> is called a '''strong Choquet space'''. Every strong Choquet space is a Choquet space, although the converse does not hold.

All nonempty [[complete metric space]]s and [[Compact space|compact]] [[Hausdorff space|T<sub>2</sub> spaces]] are strong Choquet. (In the first case, Player II, given <math>(x_i,U_i)</math>, chooses <math>V_i</math> such that <math>\operatorname{diam}(V_i)<1/i</math> and <math>\operatorname{cl}(V_i) \subseteq V_{i-1}</math>. Then the sequence <math>\left \{ x_i \right \} \to x \in V_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.) Any subset of a strong Choquet space that is a [[Gδ set|<math>G_\delta</math> set]] is strong Choquet. Metrizable spaces are [[completely metrizable]] if and only if they are strong Choquet.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Becker|first1=Howard|last2=Kechris|first2=A. S.|author2link = Alexander Kechris|title=The Descriptive Set Theory of Polish Group Actions|date=1996|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780521576055|pages=59|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L4Jf_ZRxqt8C&pg=PA59|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Kechris|first1=Alexander|title=Classical Descriptive Set Theory|date=2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9781461241904|pages=43–45|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WR3SBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA43|language=en}}</ref>
